article.title: Health Care Cuts
article.author: Mark Kreidler
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Congressional Democrats will want to burst out of the gate next year by quickly addressing the affordability issues that voters have said are critical to them, especially around health care. Then again, Donald Trump is still president. Is it gridlock? Not necessarily, some policy observers say. By skillfully deploying their majority strength in both the House and Senate, the Democrats may be able to restore some of the cuts made to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, among other programs. It’ll be arduous, and it is certainly political work. But the chance for progress is there. “I can imagine Democrats negotiating with President Trump on a partial delay of Medicaid cuts and a temporary restoration of enhanced Affordable Care Act premium subsidies,” Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at the health information site KFF, told Capital & Main. “They would likely need to agree to some concessions, like implementing some version of health [savings] accounts that Trump favors.” In some cases, Levitt said, Democrats could include such changes as part of larger “must pass” legislation like government funding bills, where they’d have the ability in both chambers to vote down the spending measures unless they got the concessions they were looking for. How Trump will react to any of that isn’t known, because how he will react to any given situation is all but impossible to predict. There’s a chance, though, that with two years left in office and his party routed in the midterms, the president finds middle ground with Democrats on some of the runaway affordability issues that could stick to his legacy. “We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country — very important,” Trump told Politico during an election-night phone interview. “I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” Related: California's Medi-Cal Crisis Deepens as Billionaire Wealth Tax Falls Short Restoring the Affordable Care Act’s enhanced subsidies, which expired last year, was a cornerstone of Democratic national campaign policy. Before the election, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) made it clear that extending the enhanced subsidies would be an early priority should his party prevail. These tax credits, part of the American Rescue Plan passed in 2021 during the COVID-19 aftermath, drove down monthly premium costs for Americans using the ACA marketplace — Obamacare — to buy their health insurance. The enhancements not only provided greater subsidies to users, but also enlarged the pool of people eligible to participate. The lower monthly bills helped to nearly double ACA enrollment from 11.7 million in 2021 to 22.3 million last year . With Republicans in control of Congress, the enhancements were allowed to expire on Dec. 31, 2025. Monthly premium costs took off, and KFF has estimated an enrollment decrease of at least 17% nationally as a result. California, which has nearly 2 million people signed up through its Covered California program, is using state subsidies to offset some of the federal cuts and keep people enrolled. But both locally and nationally, bringing back the enhanced subsidies would be a popular and welcome move. Jeffries, who intends to run for speaker of the House once the Democratic majority is sworn in on Jan. 3, has also said that his party will push hard to restore some of the deep cuts to Medicaid that were part of H.R. 1, the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The Trump administration’s signature spending bill, H.R. 1 includes a projected $1 trillion in cuts to federal funding of Medicaid programs like Medi-Cal, through which nearly 14 million low-income Californians and their families receive health care. (California’s recently defeated Prop. 40 was an attempt to backfill some of the estimated $30 billion per year in federal funding that the state is set to lose.) Democrats may look for ways to slow-roll that process by introducing a series of repeal and delay bills, which would likely prompt Trump vetoes and kickstart rounds of negotiation. But because the reductions in federal spending on Medicaid affect all states, and in many cases hammer red-leaning states because of their reliance on the program, there may be room for compromise. Related: California Saves Millions on Home Care: Workers Pay the Price These are not small swings. In the case of the Affordable Care Act subsidies, for example, the new Congress will have less than two weeks in January before the 2027 enrollment period closes. If Democrats are able to wrangle enhancements later in the year, they would likely have to make them retroactive. And that’s to say nothing of huge Democrat-led ideas like restoring enhanced Child Tax Credits, a move that was lauded for lifting 2.1 million children out of poverty in 2021 alone. Floating such ambitious legislation over the next two years would be a way for Democrats to signal their intentions for the 2028 presidential election and beyond. In the meantime, the Democratic Party is preparing to go toe to toe with a president whose administration has leaned into the idea of cutting federal government spending, even as it handed out tax breaks to the wealthy. Trump himself remains a wild card. “I expect the Democrats to try to pass their health care agenda, but they’ll likely be stymied by President Trump’s veto pen,” Levitt said. “Then it will become a game of 3-D chess to try to figure out what they can accomplish on health care that President Trump will sign.” Capital & Main
